title: Stream of Consciousness
welcome_lead: Woolf and Joyce open the doors of the mind. Trace the stream of consciousness as a modernist technique.
meta_desc: Stream of consciousness in Woolf, Joyce and modernist prose at A-Level English Literature.
final_note: You have plunged into the modernist stream and surfaced able to identify its eddies.

concepts.def: Technique presenting the unbroken flow of thought, sensation and memory (William James 1890; Joyce, Woolf).
A character's continuous unspoken thought directly rendered, often without quotation marks.
Third-person narration adopting a character's idiom — central modernist tool for inwardness.
Woolf's 1925 novel weaving multiple consciousnesses across a single London day.
Joyce's 1922 novel rewriting Homer across 18 episodes of Dublin, with shifting techniques.
Joyce's term for a sudden revelation of essence within the ordinary.

walkthroughs.body_html:
William James coined stream of consciousness in 1890 to describe the continuous flow of mental life.

Modernist novelists found in it a way to capture interiority that realist conventions had elided.
Woolf moves between Clarissa, Septimus, Peter and others, weaving their thoughts across a single day. Free indirect discourse lets one paragraph house several voices.
Ulysses ends with Molly Bloom's unpunctuated monologue — eight long sentences and one final yes. The stream becomes a flood.
